title: Ancient and Polynesian Voyaging
description: Phoenicians, Polynesians, and the Vikings — long before the Age of Discovery

concepts.title: The Phoenician Mediterranean
concepts.contentHtml:
The Phoenicians, based in city-states along the modern Lebanese coast (Tyre, Sidon, Byblos), were the dominant seafarers of the Iron Age Mediterranean from roughly 1200–500 BCE. Their cedar-built ships and skilled celestial navigation took them around the entire Mediterranean and out beyond the Pillars of Hercules — the Strait of Gibraltar — into the Atlantic.

According to Herodotus, around 600 BCE the Egyptian pharaoh Necho II commissioned a Phoenician fleet to circumnavigate Africa. The expedition reportedly took three years, planting and harvesting crops along the way, and returned via the Strait of Gibraltar. Whether the account is accurate is debated, but the navigational details — including a shadow-cast pattern that would only be observed south of the equator — are surprisingly hard to fake.

The Phoenicians founded colonies across the Mediterranean — most famously Carthage (in modern Tunisia) — and traded for Cornish tin, North African gold, and Iberian silver. The alphabet they developed for commerce became the ancestor of Greek, Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, and Cyrillic.

concepts.title: Polynesian Voyaging
concepts.contentHtml:
The greatest sustained feat of pre-modern seafaring was the Polynesian expansion across roughly 25 million km² of the Pacific Ocean, an area about the size of North America.

From a homeland in the area of Taiwan and Southeast Asia, Austronesian-speaking peoples gradually voyaged outward in double-hulled outrigger canoes built without metal tools and capable of carrying livestock, plants, and several dozen people.

  • Tonga and Samoa were settled by ~900 BCE.
  • The Marquesas, Society Islands, and Hawai'i by ~700–1000 CE.
  • Easter Island (Rapa Nui) by ~1200 CE.
  • Aotearoa (New Zealand) was the last major landmass on Earth to be settled by humans, around 1280 CE.

Polynesian navigators used celestial observations, wave patterns, bird behaviour, and cloud formations to find tiny islands across thousands of kilometres of open ocean — without compass, sextant, or written charts. Modern reconstructions like the Hawaiian voyaging canoe Hokule'a have circumnavigated the Pacific (and the world) using only traditional methods, vindicating their accuracy.

concepts.title: Vikings and the North Atlantic
concepts.contentHtml:
From around 793 CE (the raid on Lindisfarne) to the late 11th century, the Vikings from Scandinavia conducted a remarkable expansion by sea — combining trade, settlement, and raiding.

Their open-decked clinker-built longships could be sailed in open ocean and rowed up rivers, giving them unmatched flexibility. Key moves:

  • Settled Iceland from ~870.
  • Settled Greenland from ~985 (Erik the Red).
  • Reached Vinland in North America by ~1000 (L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is the only confirmed Norse site there). The settlement was abandoned within a few decades.
  • To the east, Swedish Vikings (the Rus') established trade routes to Constantinople via the river systems of modern Russia and Ukraine — and gave Russia its name.

Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage was therefore not the first European contact with the Americas — but it was the first that led to sustained transatlantic contact.

title: The Age of Discovery
description: Henry the Navigator, Columbus, da Gama, and Magellan

concepts.title: Portugal Begins
concepts.contentHtml:
The European Age of Discovery (roughly 1415–1600) was launched by Portugal, a small Atlantic-facing country whose voyages were sponsored by Prince Henry the Navigator (1394–1460; his famous 'navigation school' at Sagres is largely legend). Henry never voyaged himself but funded a systematic exploration southward along the African coast.

Portuguese caravels — small, manoeuvrable lateen-rigged ships that could sail close to the wind — pushed each year a little further south. Cape Bojador, long feared as the edge of the navigable world, was rounded in 1434. Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, finally proving Africa could be circumnavigated. Vasco da Gama reached India in May 1498, opening a sea route that bypassed the Venetian and Mamluk-controlled routes through the Middle East and reshaped Eurasian commerce.

Within a few decades the Portuguese had established trading posts from Mozambique to Hormuz to Goa to Malacca to Macau, controlling the Indian Ocean spice trade and dramatically lowering the cost of pepper, cloves, and nutmeg in European markets.

concepts.title: Columbus and the Atlantic Crossing
concepts.contentHtml:
Convinced — wrongly — that the Earth was small enough that Asia could be reached by sailing west, the Genoese sailor Christopher Columbus (1451–1506) secured Spanish crown backing in 1492 from Ferdinand and Isabella, fresh from completing the Reconquista.

His three-ship expedition (Santa María, Pinta, Niña) made landfall in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492. Columbus believed until his death that he had reached Asia. The Caribbean islands he encountered were home to indigenous peoples — primarily the Taíno — whose subsequent encounter with European diseases, slavery, and warfare collapsed their populations within decades.

The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, which adjusted a line drawn by Pope Alexander VI in 1493, divided non-European lands between Spain and Portugal along a meridian roughly 370 leagues west of Cape Verde. The treaty allotted most of the Americas to Spain — and Brazil (then unknown) to Portugal, which is why Brazil today speaks Portuguese while the rest of Latin America speaks Spanish.

concepts.title: Magellan and the First Circumnavigation
concepts.contentHtml:
The first circumnavigation of the globe was led by the Portuguese sailor Ferdinand Magellan, in service to Spain. His expedition departed in September 1519 with five ships and 270 men.

The voyage was extraordinary in difficulty. They found the strait through southern South America that now bears Magellan's name; crossed the Pacific so vast and empty that the crew suffered scurvy and starvation; reached the Philippines, where Magellan was killed in a skirmish in April 1521. Only one ship, the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, completed the round trip — arriving back in Spain in September 1522 with 18 of the original 270 men.

The voyage revealed the true size of the Earth, and that the world was a single, connected ocean. The discoveries of the Pacific's vastness, of the strait, and of routes to the Spice Islands transformed the geopolitics of the 16th century. Within decades the Manila Galleon trade carried silver from Acapulco to Manila in exchange for Chinese silks, completing a global commercial circuit for the first time in history.

title: Charting the Pacific
description: Cook, Bering, longitude, and the scientific voyage

concepts.title: The Longitude Problem
concepts.contentHtml:
For two centuries after Magellan, sailors could measure their latitude easily — by the noon altitude of the sun, or the elevation of Polaris — but had no reliable way to measure their longitude at sea. The result was repeated catastrophic shipwrecks; in 1707, four British warships ran aground at the Scilly Isles, killing nearly 2,000 sailors.

Britain's 1714 Longitude Act offered £20,000 — a fortune — for a method accurate to half a degree. Two competing approaches:

  • Lunar distances — comparing the moon's position against stars and using astronomical tables. Accurate but mathematically demanding.
  • The marine chronometer — a clock accurate enough to keep Greenwich time after months at sea, allowing longitude to be calculated from the difference between local noon and Greenwich time.

The Yorkshire clockmaker John Harrison built a series of remarkable clocks (H1, H2, H3, H4) over four decades. His H4 (1759) — about the size of a pocket watch — kept time within a few seconds over a transatlantic voyage. After much resistance from the Board of Longitude, Harrison was finally rewarded by Parliament in 1773, in his old age, though never formally awarded the prize itself.

concepts.title: Captain Cook's Three Voyages
concepts.contentHtml:
Captain James Cook (1728–1779) of the Royal Navy carried the new instruments — Harrison's chronometer K1, a copy of H4 — into the Pacific on the most consequential scientific voyages of the 18th century.

  • First voyage (1768–71) — observed the transit of Venus from Tahiti, charted the coast of New Zealand and the eastern coast of Australia. Joseph Banks's botanical collection from Botany Bay was the foundation of European knowledge of Australasian flora.
  • Second voyage (1772–75) — sailed deep into the Antarctic Circle, the first ship to do so, and demonstrated that no large temperate southern continent existed.
  • Third voyage (1776–79) — searched for a Northwest Passage from the Pacific side, charted the coasts from Oregon to Alaska, and visited the Hawaiian Islands. Cook was killed at Kealakekua Bay in February 1779 during a confrontation with Native Hawaiians.

Cook's voyages were models of disciplined seamanship and navigation. He all but eliminated scurvy on his ships through fresh provisions and citrus, mapped vast stretches of coastline with high accuracy, and exemplified the new style of scientific exploration.

concepts.title: Bering, La Pérouse, and the Russian Pacific
concepts.contentHtml:
The North Pacific was charted in parallel by Russian and French expeditions:

  • Danish-born Vitus Bering, commissioned by Peter the Great and later Empress Anna, led two great Kamchatka expeditions (1725–30 and 1733–43). The first sailed through the strait now bearing his name in 1728; the second reached Alaska in 1741, charted the Aleutians and Alaska, and effectively claimed the region for Russia. Bering himself died of scurvy on a desert island in 1741.
  • French explorer Jean-François de Galaup, Comte de La Pérouse (1741–88) led an ambitious scientific circumnavigation in two ships (Boussole and Astrolabe). They charted Korea, Japan, the Russian Far East, and Australia before disappearing without trace in the South Pacific in 1788. The wreckage was found at Vanikoro in 1827, and the full story of the disaster remains incomplete.

By 1800, almost the entire Pacific Rim had been charted, the major island groups were known to European cartographers, and the era of 'unknown' coasts in temperate waters was effectively closed.

title: The Polar Heroic Age
description: Amundsen, Scott, Shackleton, and the race for the poles

concepts.title: The North Pole
concepts.contentHtml:
Reaching the geographic poles became one of the great scientific and nationalist obsessions of the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

The North Pole attracted the first decades of effort. Major attempts:

  • Norwegian Fridtjof Nansen deliberately allowed his ship Fram to be locked in Arctic ice (1893–96), aiming to drift across the pole. He didn't reach it but pioneered Arctic survival techniques.
  • American Frederick Cook claimed the pole in 1908 and Robert Peary in 1909 — both contested and now generally not accepted.
  • Norwegian Roald Amundsen, with airship Norge, made the first verifiable overflight of the pole in 1926.
  • The Soviet expedition of 1948 was the first verified ground arrival.
  • Wally Herbert's 1968–69 expedition made the first surface crossing of the Arctic Ocean via the pole (with air resupply).

Arctic exploration also produced the first navigations of the Northwest Passage (Amundsen, 1903–06, with the Gjøa) and the Northeast Passage (Nordenskiöld, 1878–79, with the Vega) — sea routes long sought by European traders for shorter access to Asia.

concepts.title: Race to the South Pole
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1911–12 race to the South Pole remains one of exploration's most dramatic episodes.

  • Roald Amundsen (Norway), with a small, expert team using sled dogs and skis, reached the pole on 14 December 1911. All five men returned safely.
  • Robert Falcon Scott (Britain), relying on man-hauling and motor sledges, reached the pole on 17 January 1912 — five weeks too late, only to find Amundsen's tent and flag. Scott and his four companions died on the return march, just 18 km from a supply depot. His diary, recovered the following spring, became one of the great tragic documents of exploration.

The contrast between Amundsen's careful preparation and Scott's mixed methods has been studied as a case in leadership and logistics ever since. Amundsen had set up depots, used dogs efficiently, eaten dogs as planned to reduce weight, and chosen a shorter route. Scott's expedition had multiple competing technologies, scientific obligations, and bad weather — but the gap was as much in management as in fortune.

concepts.title: Shackleton and the Endurance
concepts.contentHtml:
The most extraordinary survival story of the polar age belongs to Ernest Shackleton's 1914–17 Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition.

The plan was to cross Antarctica via the South Pole. The expedition ship Endurance was trapped in pack ice in the Weddell Sea before reaching the continent (January 1915), drifted for ten months, was crushed by ice and sank in November 1915. The 28-man crew survived on the ice for five months, eventually launching the ship's lifeboats and reaching the desolate Elephant Island.

Shackleton then led a six-man crew in the small lifeboat James Caird on an 800 nautical mile open-boat voyage across the Southern Ocean to South Georgia — navigating with sextant in storms that should have swamped them. Once landed on the wrong side of South Georgia, Shackleton, Worsley, and Crean made the first crossing of its glaciated mountains. Shackleton then organised a rescue from Chile that returned to Elephant Island and brought the entire crew home — without losing a single man on the main party.

The Endurance wreck, located by sonar in March 2022 some 3,000 m below the Weddell Sea ice, was found astonishingly well preserved.

title: Modern Frontiers
description: The deep ocean, space, and what it means to explore today

concepts.title: The Deep Ocean
concepts.contentHtml:
By the mid-20th century the planet's surface was largely mapped, but its oceans — covering 70 % of Earth's surface and reaching nearly 11 km deep — remained almost entirely unknown.

Major milestones:

  • 1872–76 — HMS Challenger expedition, the first systematic global oceanographic survey, founded modern oceanography and discovered the Mariana Trench.
  • 1960 — bathyscaphe Trieste with Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended to 10,916 m in the Challenger Deep — for over fifty years, the only crewed dive to the bottom.
  • 1977: discovery of hydrothermal vents on the Galápagos Rift, complete with chemoautotrophic ecosystems independent of sunlight: a fundamental revision of where and how life can exist.
  • 2012 — James Cameron solo-piloted Deepsea Challenger to the bottom of the Mariana Trench.
  • 2018–19: Victor Vescovo's Five Deeps Expedition reached the deepest point in each of the world's five oceans.

Yet about three-quarters of the seafloor remains unmapped at high resolution (Seabed 2030 reported roughly a quarter mapped in 2024). The deep ocean is still the largest unexplored region of Earth.

concepts.title: Space Exploration
concepts.contentHtml:
The Cold War turned space into the new frontier of exploration:

  • 1957 — Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite in orbit; Sputnik 2 carried the dog Laika.
  • 1961 — Yuri Gagarin on Vostok 1 became the first human in space.
  • 1969 — Apollo 11 landed Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon. Twelve men have walked on the Moon, all American, all between 1969 and 1972.
  • 1971 — Mars 3 became the first spacecraft to soft-land on Mars.
  • 1977 onward — Voyager 1 and 2 conducted the grand tour of the outer planets, with the first close-ups of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012 — the most distant human-made object.
  • 1998–today — the International Space Station, continuously crewed since November 2000, the most ambitious peaceful international engineering project in history.
  • 2020s — return to crewed lunar exploration with NASA's Artemis programme, Mars rovers (Perseverance), commercial crew via SpaceX, and exoplanet science via JWST.

concepts.title: What Is Left to Discover?
concepts.contentHtml:
Geographic exploration is largely complete in the simple sense — every coastline is charted, every major mountain peak has been climbed (the last 8000-metre summit, Shisha Pangma, was first reached in 1964). But the more interesting frontiers are now scientific:

  • The deep oceans — still largely unmapped at fine resolution, hosting unknown species at every dive.
  • The Earth's interior — the deepest borehole, the Kola Superdeep, only reaches 12.3 km, less than 0.2 % of the way to the centre.
  • The Solar System — many bodies (Mars, Europa, Enceladus, Titan) plausibly harbour habitable subsurface oceans; biosignature missions are in early development.
  • The exoplanets — over 5,000 confirmed since 1995, with potential biosignature observations possible within decades.
  • Life itself — the genomes of most micro-organisms, deep-sea life, and even soil microbiomes remain largely uncatalogued.

Exploration in the 21st century is less about reaching new places and more about asking new questions in places we already know — and reckoning with the cumulative impact our explorations have had on the people and ecosystems already there.
